newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany to overshoot 1996 borrowing target.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany to overshoot 1996 borrowing target.

text.p: Germany admitted on Thursday that delays in its privatisation programme will hit government revenues in 1996, pushing it over a borrowing target already jacked up once by Finance Minister Theo Waigel.
Sources in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative coalition said new borrowing would bust a limit of 70 billion marks ($45.70 billion) by another five to 10 billion marks.
The original borrowing target was 60 billion marks, but was missed when Waigel recently topped up Germany's unemployment benefits scheme -- burdened by nearly four million jobless.
Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) slammed Waigel's failure to stick to the target, accusing him of deception and even of flying in the face of the German constitution.
"Waigel has totally lost control of the 1996 budget," SPD finance spokeswoman Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier said in a statement.
Economists were less worried, however, noting that under the Maastricht Treaty on European economic and monetary union (EMU), privatisation revenues are not included in calculating the deficit.
The treaty says that countries wanting to join the single European currency's launch in 1999 must limit budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997.
"This is neutral for the deficit as defined by Maastricht," economist Thomas Mayer at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt said.
But the admission is a blow for the credibility of Waigel's financial policy, so important when Germany is seen as forming the cornerstone of the single currency.
"Waigel gambled and guessed revenues too high," Ruetger Teuscher, economist at Deutsche Bank Research, told Reuters.

A finance ministry spokesman said it was still too early to predict final new borrowing requirements this year. But plans for a 1996 budget deficit of 3.5 percent of GDP and 2.5 percent in 1997 were still intact.

Teuscher said that would be tough. Even scraping under three percent in 1997 would require further savings on top of a 70 billion mark austerity package whose welfare cuts have already aroused the anger of trade unionists.
"Three percent can only be done under positive assumptions, depending on further savings or higher-than-expected revenues," Teuscher said.

Maastricht also sets a national debt target of 60 percent of GDP -- although it may be loosely interpreted in terms of countries reducing their debt towards the limit. Debt levels will be measured at the end of 1997, so if the privatisations go ahead next year the net impact in Germany would be minimal.
"The debt quota will rise more than expected this year and fall more than expected next year. But the level at the end of 1997 will be little changed," Mayer said.
The SPD, quoting a finance ministry report, told parliament on Wednesday the government would see hardly any of the planned nine billion marks in privatisation revenues this year.
Sales of a Frankfurt property company, Postbank AG and a share in Lufthansa AG all look doubtful, it said.

Matthaeus-Maier said the government would, under the German constitution, have to admit that economic stability had been lost before new borrowing can exceed state investment, set this year at 66 billion marks.
But the finance ministry said the clause only applied to the drafting of the budget, not its implementation. -- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150 ($1=1.5315 Mark)
